Reprinted From 
The Bulletin of 
The Institute of Child Study 
University of Toronto 


“FASTER 

FASTER” 

Mary L, Northway 


“Now, now”, cried the Queen, “Faster, 
faster!” 

You may remember that after Alice 
had run as fast as she could she found 
herself under the same tree she had 
started from. “In our cdiii^try”, said 
Alice, “You’d generally get to some¬ 
where else, if you ran very fast for a 
long time”. 

“A slow sort of country”, said the 
Queen. “Now here it takes all the 
running you can do to keep in the 
same place. If you want to get some¬ 
where else, you must run twice as fast 
as that.” ' 


We seem to have become used to 
living in the “Looking Glass” country 
ourselves. We not only go faster and 
faster, but we feel there is some 
moral virtue in so doing. We boast 
that we have driven 3200 miles in 
six days, but say little of what we 
saw on the way. We are proud of 
attending ten committee meetings in 
a week, but hate to admit we enjoyed 
any of them. We exult in the fact that 
we obtained our Ph.D. or became 
assistant manager at an earlier age than 
any other candidate. Conversely, we 
feel slightly apologetic to admit that 
we spent an evening sitting at home, 
and if we do find time to “stand and 
stare” we assume that it is a sin to 
waste time, but not to waste energy. 
Like the busy bee we feel we must im¬ 
prove each shining hour, forgetting 
that the bee is more conscious of the 
sunshine and the nectar than of his 
efforts at self or social improvement. 
Our race to “get on”, to come first, to 
get ahead, usually takes us back to the 
same tree, having achieved only breath¬ 
lessness, fatigue, ulcers or a neurosis on 
the way, and having no time whatever 
to enjoy the view. However, the Faster- 
Faster principle is deeply embedded in 
our cultural pattern, and if we adults 
choose to ride on • a continuously 
accelerating merry-go-roiind, it is our 
business. We obtain the illusion of pro¬ 
gress; if we are fast enough we may 
even catch the “ring” in which case 
we can travel onward again, until 
finally we become at best bored, and at 
worst dizzy. But when we put our 
children on the merry-go-round we all 
too often drive them to; nothing but 
distraction. When we force tfiem to run 
Faster-Faster they become anxious, 
fatigued and a little crabby. They 
would rather have spent the time play¬ 
ing by the tree which was pleasant 
itself in the first pilace. 


8 


Canadian Camping 




Parents hurry children and judge 
their worth according to a law of con¬ 
servation of time and expenditure of 
energy. The child who can read at 
five years is deemed better than the 
child who reads at six, even though 
they both read only comics. The child 
who has made many friends is better 
than the child who has made a few. 
The child who violates the folkways of 
“getting on with the job” by dawdling 
is considered to present a problem so 
serious that it requires special con¬ 
sideration at parent education meet¬ 
ings. To help them conform to the 
Faster-Faster principle we arrange each 
hour we can with worth-while activ¬ 
ities, music lessons, dancing classes, 
iraining in sports, art classes, extra 
reading and supervised play. 

But parents are no more inculcated 
with the hurry-up approach than 
psychologists. For years these scientists 
have been conducting experiments on 
learning both with children and ani¬ 
mals. In these they have assumed, 
unquestionably, that learning can be 
evaluated in terms of its speed. Rats 
who are slow in learning to find the 
cheese, or children who take a long 
time in learning vulgar fractions, are 
said to be stupid. No one even suspects 
that they may simply have been wise 
enough to know that both cheeses and 
fractions would wait and that there 
were many more interesting things to 
do and to see en route to these laudable 
goals. 

It is too much to suggest that we all 
stop running and sit under the tree 
where we are: such an atomic idea 
would disrupt our cultural pattern 
more drastically than an invasion. We 
will continue to hurry and our children 
will hurry to keep up with us, and 
then we will hurry to keep up with our 
children. But without being considered 


insurgents could we hesitantly advocate 
a Freedom-from-Hurry plan to be 
effective only for playtime and holi¬ 
days? Could play become play again 
instead of “organised recreation”? 
Could camps provide periods for 
dabbling and dawdling, instead of days 
filled with instructional periods and 
interest groups? Could we abolish 
badges for achievement and bestow 
them for enjoyment? Could we pro¬ 
claim one day a year on which every 
one did exactly as he liked, and even 
the clocks ceased to run? Could we 
give our children, if not ourselves, the 
privilege of believing that it is the 
process not the product that is im¬ 
portant, the journeying as much as 
the destination that has significance? 
Could we help them to discover that 
they learn to live, not live to learn? 
Can’t the curriculum of living provide 
its real recesses? 

Such thoughts are not mere facetious 
wanderings of the imagination. We 
seriously feel that the tremendous pres¬ 
sures places on the child of today to 
“get on”, to “make good”, to “do 
well”, to “maintain and surpass stand¬ 
ards”, place heavy strains on his sound 
healthy development. The child learns, 
all too easily, to conform as we en¬ 
courage him to run Faster-Faster. In 
doing so he often misses the beauty of 
the world around him, and in the end 
he may discover the prizes of the race 
are only baubles; or the strain on his 
psychological muscles may be too 
great and so he becomes a deformed 
or broken creature. 

Perhaps we cannot teach ourselves, 
but we might teach our children that 
the worst waste of time is never to 
waste time, and that incessant nmning 
takes you back to the same tree—the 
only difference being that you are now 
both hot and thirsty. 

—• 


Toronto, Canada, December 1962

WHY I DIRECT A CAMP 

By Don Groff, 

Director of Youth and Camping, 
Kitchener-Waterloo YMCA 


I have delayed writing this article 
because like all human beings I find the 
prospect of self-evaluation and intro¬ 
spection of one’s motives a frightening 
one. And yet it is a healthy prospect to 
examine one’s motives whenever one 
undertakes any venture in life. There is 
a magic in camping that captures the 
imagination of men and women. Cer¬ 
tainly any who have spent any time at 
all in positions of camp leadership, and 
more particularly, those of senior 
responsibility, would attest to the truth 
contained in that statement. That 
which follows, then, is the result of 
one such person’s reflection upon the 
])lace of camping in his life. 

Camping among other things in¬ 
volves a geographic location. To separ¬ 
ate any consideration of one’s motive in 
directing a camp from the unicjue 
features of the location would he eejuiv- 
alent to divesting a tree of its roots. 
For, it is from the setting of a summer 
camp that one derives inspiration for 
the very life of the camp. God’s great 
out-of-doors provides stimulation for 
the imagination of any director. A 
cabin, nestled in a grove of trees is a 
call to ad\enturous living, but trans¬ 
planted to the concrete jungle of our 
cities it would be labelled a shack, 
hazardous probablv to healthy urban 
living. No, as a director I could not 
perform elsewhere the same as I do 
under the ojx'n skies at camp. 

Coupled with the .setting and closely 
allied to it, is the primitive existence 


which camping provides for its parti¬ 
cipants. The inter-dependency of those 
who find themselves within a camp 
setting creates an atmosphere of in¬ 
formality and naturalness, which seems 
to allow people to be themselves. 
Position, status .symbols, household 
conveniences and those things which 
we have come to rely upon in our 
modern social existence mean little 
when paddling a canoe, or cleaning a 
cabin floor, or cooking a meal for a 
camp group. Somehow we are able to 
get closer to one another at camp, and 
somehow we a»'e able to feel free to 
be ourselves. From tins informality, 
from this sense of freedom, we as 
campers are able to release potential 
which otherwise remains stifled by the 
jjressures of modern .social living. As 
one concerned with the development of 
young people and the growth and 
maturing of our society, the author sees 
camp as an opportunity for assisting 
IxMsons to be their own best selves. 

'Fhen too, camping gives opportun- 
itv for seiA'ing one’s fellow man. By 
means of the tasks which a director 
iMM-forms daily and indeed through his 
efTorts in the preparation for any given 
season, he is able to render his unic|ue 
contribution to the stafT team which in 
turn provides the total operation of 
tlnat season at camp. Secondly he. 
through his personal contact with 
members of the staff' and camper per-

Le Camp Ecole Trois-Saumons 
et Ses Camps de Formation 

liienvenue! The Editorial Committee welcomes our first article in French. 
Encore s'il vous plait! 


Foncic en 1947, Ic Canip-Ecole IVois- 
Saunions troiiva difficilenicnt a cette 
cpocjue, les pcrsonnes competentes pour 
renscigneiiient dc la natation et le 
maniemcnt des embarcations ainsi qiie 
pour Tenseigneinent dcs sciences natu- 
rcllcs. La generositc de son personnel ne 
lui fit jamais defaut, inais la prepara¬ 
tion immediate, Tinitiation et la com¬ 
petence particulicre que dcmande la 
vie dc Camp, fiirent souvent loin des 
espoirs fondes. 

C’est a la solution de ces divers 
problemes que s’attaque successive- 
ment le Camp, des que ses structures 
internes le lui permirent, que Torgani- 
sation inaterielle des locaux fut ade¬ 
quate. 

Natation et Sccurite aquatique 

L’Ecole provinciale dc natation fut 
fondee en 1949, avec une section 
anglaise et une section frangaise. Le 
programme suivi est celui de la Socicte 
canadienne de la Croix-Rouge. A date, 
1.") cours ont etc donnes, suivis par 1503 
stagiaires dont 759 re^urent leur dip- 
lome d'instructeur. La natation, le 
inanieinent des embarcations Icgeres et 
la securitc aquatique en general, sont 
enseignes. La qualification senior est 
exigible pour radmission. 

Sciences naturelles

Plante, en charge de cette responsabilite 
au Camp, trouva-t-il les aides eclaires 


necessaires! — Et il fallait penser a 
Tavenir et preparer une releve. M.

Dix cours de quin/e jours, dix de 
dix jours, ont ete organises depuis, et

A Build "It "Yourself 

Switnming Pool 

], C, Moore 

Boy Scouts of Canada 


“A swimming pool for our camp? 
Well, a camp doesn’t seem complete 
without somewhere to swim, but surely 
an artificial swimming pool is beyond 
our budget.” In how many camp com¬ 
mittee meetings have these thoughts 
been expressed! Even where a lake or 
river is available, we wistfully recog¬ 
nize that an artificial swiming pool 
has advantages and offers a longer 
season. Is it too expensive? Let me tell 
you how we met this challenge. 

Neither our need and desire for a 
pool, nor our solution to our problem 
are original. We had for some time felt 
the need, and had collected informa¬ 
tion and data on designs of pools and 
methods of construction. We found that 
the size of pool we required was far 
beyond the limited funds available. 

It was a magazine article by Frank¬ 
lin Folsom entitled “Full Size Pool for 
Only $300” that started a member of 
our Camp Committee planning and 
dreaming of the day when we would 
have a swimming pol at camp. “You 
can build a 20’ x 20’ swimming pool 
for less than $300” was the opening 
sentence. It went on to tell of “The 
enthusiastic fans reporting excellent 
service from such pools in places as 
diverse as western New York, Virginia, 
Texas, southern New Mexico and 
northern Massachusetts.” “Some of the 
pools are drained, cleaned and refilled 
from two to four times a season.” “If 
water is limited you may need to add 
the cost of a recirculating filter to the 
original figure. ... In one 50,000 


gallon pool I know of, a $200 filter 
has served well.” 

The pools in diverse places men¬ 
tioned above all apparently were the 
outcome of a previous magazine article 
by Mr. Folsom back in 1944 written 
after he had built and successfully 
used his own pool for a period of five 
years. What is the secret? “The 
method has been successfully used for 
many years as a quick, inexpensive 
way of building farm ponds, canals, 
and dams, but so far as I know, my 
wife and I were the first to apply the 
technique to a swimming pool” states 
Mr. Folsom. “You dig a hole, line it 
with asphalt impregnated strips, 
cement them together and they form a 
tough watertight bottom.” 

There was some skepticism in the 
minds of members of our Committee. 
The statement that 40’ x 50’ pools 
were said to be built for less than $200 
could well create some doiibt. There 
was, however, admirable optimism, 
persistence and the ability to visualize 
and overcome problems and difficulties 
on the part of other members. Certain¬ 
ly there were problems to be met and 
solved. 

The original magazine article backed 
up detailed instructions of “how to do 
it” with accounts of the success others 
had in following this method. One item 
that was of special interest to us was 
the statement that “Perhaps the biggest 
asphalt-strip pool on record is George 
J. Rupprecht’s 40’ x 70’ jumbo in 
Burlington, Mass. ... He operates a 
day camp and for the past 10 years 


12 


Canadian Camping 



durinij; the summer 300 children and 
adults have been splashing in it every 
day. ... A pool in New \'ork has been 
used lor 10 vears as a winter skating 
rink.” 

Planning, estimating of local costs 
and incorporating features to meet 
local conditions and needs occupied 
many sessions of our Committee. Fol¬ 
lowing Mr. Folsom’s detailed directions 
with .some alterations to adapt his 
method to our needs and conditions, 
we felt that a 30’ x 61’ pool could be 
built lor around $2000, provided we 
used careful budgeting and a great deal 
of voluntary labour. Care must be 
taken in selecting the .site of the pool 
— one with a plentiful supply of water 
and a means of disposing of water 
when emptying the pool. It should be in 
a location that allows the sun to warm 
the water. Trees too clo.se overhead 
have a tendency to dioj) l(‘aves, seeds 
and insects into the pool. 

T he site we cho.se was on le\ el sandy 
.soil, close to the edge ol a steep slope 
dropjnng down to the ri\’er 50 feet 
below from which we could obtain a 
plentiful water supply, not only for 
original tilling, but to compensate for 
evaporation, backwashing filters, etc. 


Except for the original excavation 
for the pool, all work was done by 



hand by volunteers. Care was taken, 
therefore to have the bulldozer leave 
the bottom ol the excavation as level 
and smooth as possible and conforming 
to our planned depths of 3 feet at the 
shallow end and 6 feet at the other. 
Excavated material was placed care¬ 
fully around the perimeter of the hole, 
forming a rim 18” high. The pool is 
thus partially above the level of the 
surrounding area which helps prevent 
leaves and other debris being carried 
into the pool by winds. 

A standard screened drain fitting 
was secured and cast into a 4” thick 
concrete slab which was placed in the 
lowest spot in the centre of the ex¬ 
cavation. Phistic pipe for filling, drain¬ 
ing, filtering and chlorinating was 
j)laced in jK)sition and buried under¬ 
ground, the ends leading to an adjacent 
pump house. Rakes and shovels were 
used to finish levelling, smoothing and 
tamping the bottom and sides of the 
pool. Th.e sides and ends cannot be 
made vertical; in this type of pool they 
should conform to a l-to-1 pitch or 
angle of about 45 degrees or there¬ 
abouts depending somewhat on the 
nature of the soil. A transit level or 
other accurate means should be used to 
ensure that the bottom, sides, ends, 
deptlis and rim are absolutely level 
and conform to your plans. 

Many of the original pools we studied 
were lined with 90-pound roofing: 
.some even had roofing with a coloured 
slate finish on the top layer. We de¬ 
cided upon canal liner which is con¬ 
structed of asphalt and asbestos and 
should have a longer life. 

As the next procedure began, work- 
eis were cautioned to wear old clothes 
and .soft-soled rubber shoes. The first 
strip of canal liner was rolled into

Five steps to the introduction of 


SCUBA Dime 

John Ruse, 

Aqua-Lun" of Cnnada 
with comment by 
C. B Davis 
Canadian Red Cross 


as a 
CAMP 


ACT/my 


Modern ingenuity has made a tech¬ 
nique centuries old referred to as 
SCUBA diving available to thousands 
of Canadians. These enthusiasts equip¬ 
ped with the latest in self-contained 
underwater breathing apparatus are 
exploring our oceans, lakes, rivers and 
cjuarries. This phenomenal growth of 
underwater h u m a n population and 
their fascinating stories of this “silent 
world” must invariably draw the 
attention of the camp director. 

Some, camp directors are today 
viewing this activity with increased 
interest, apprehension and deep con¬ 
cern for the responsibilities involved. 
Others pressured by campers to include 
this, or phases of this sport as an 
integral part of a water safety program 
arc a]Dpalled by what may appear to be 
a lack of professional advice. Such 
concern is increased by stories of the 
“terrors of the deep”, divers bends, air 
embolisms, drownings, squeezes, rap¬ 
tures of the deep, burst ear drums, are 
a few of the “interest stoppens” one 
may hear. No claim is made that these 
alTlictions do not exist but any camp 
director who has the confidence to 
undertake a program of teaching youth 
to paddle a canoe has the basic require¬ 
ments in conjunction with knowledge 
and experience to teach the use of 
SCUBA with confidence and safety. 

Knowledge and experience places 
these “terrors of the deep” in their 
|)roper perspective and demonstrates 
that tliey need be of little concern to 


the camp director. I am sure that a 
flying student today is not burdened 
with all the terrors of space travel in 
his desire to fly to ten thousand feet. 

We have in Canada today through 
the Underwater Society of America, 
the Ontario Underwater Council, the 
National Association of Underwater 
Intructors, tlic YMCA, manufacturers 
and other recognized agencies, a wealth 
of information available to the camp 
director. 

The first consideration in deciding 
whether SCUBA is a suitable activity 
for the camp is an outline of the 
advantages and disadvantages followed 
by a ste}^ by step consideration of 
factors of safety, facilities, types of 
equipment, costs and return on invest¬ 
ment. 

ADV'ANTACiES: Th.e advantages of 
this activity are limited only by the 
imagination of the director. This 
physically healthful and mentally 
stimulating sport is one in which the 
little fellow may participate on equal 
footing with the biggest. It opens many 
doors of interest to observ’ations of 
game fish to more basic fascination of 
oceanography, it is the closest proxima- 
tion to the weightlessness of the astro¬ 
naut that many of us earth bound 
will experience. It is a master teacher 
of self confidence and responsibility to 
the physical safety of a “buddy”, it is 
an introduction to certain physiological 
phenomena and demonstrates man's 


14 


Canadian Camping 


adaptability to another environment, 
certain laws of physics and the use of 
simple mathematics become alive and 
meaningful. 

Such ad\antages must, however, be 
placed in perspective with considera¬ 
tion of responsibility, problems of the 
intelligent direction of the program, 
costs and return on investment. 

In that some locations arc more 
practical than others the following five 
steps are suggested as a guide upon 
which certain decisions can be made. 

Step 1. Pro\ide for qualified in¬ 
struction. The instructor must be 
thoroughly trained, experienced, and 
we strongly recommend he or she 
possess a certificate, recognized by the 
Underwater Society of America or the 
VMCA. 

Step 2. Make jirovision for medical 
examination of e v e r y participant. 
Medical standards with particular res¬ 
pect to heart, lungs, cars and sinu.ses 
have been determined, — these require¬ 
ments are available through the Under¬ 
water Society of America, The Royal 
Canadian Navy, The Ontario Work¬ 
men’s Compensation Board, or the 
VMCA. 

Step 3. A qualified instructor should 
jiersonally swim the area to designate 
specific areas where the instruction 
and underwater activity should take 
place. In addition to bottom conditions 
an evaluation should be made of sur¬ 
face facilities and their suitability to 
this activity. 

Step 4. The instructor should make 
a list of his inventory requirements in¬ 
cluding cost and availability of air. A 
quotation may then be obtained from a 
dealer who may sell or rent the equip¬ 
ment. If the dealer has had little 
experience in this type of application 
it may be well under the circumstances 
to contact the manufacturer for his 


recommendations and advice, particu¬ 
larly in respect to depreciation and 
maintenance costs.

ginative and educational programs. 
Maintain group discipline and care¬ 
fully ob.seiN’e all rules of safety. 

If such a program is developed, it 
is considered that a valuable extra 
activity will be provided for children 
12 and over which will reflect satis¬ 
faction on the part of the camp in that 
they have contributed to the safety 
and de\'elo|jment of the camper and 
have provided a never to be forgotten 
experience which will in future years 
develop and broaden.

Mr, and 3Mrs, Lome E, Brown of Vancouver 

Theme Speakers for Canadian Camping Association Conference 
By: W, D. Smith 


The Alberta Camping Association 
in cooperation with the Recreation and 
Cultural Development Branch of the 
Government of Alberta will be host to 
the Canadian Camping Association at 
the sixth annual Camp Directors’ 
Seminar in Banff, Alberta from 
January 23rd to 26th, 1963. Professor 
and Mrs. Lome E. Brown, who are 
owner-directors of Camp Deka, will be 
the theme speakers for the conference. 

Mr. Brown is a professor in the 
Faculty and College of Education at 
the University of British Columbia. He 
is a graduate in Health and Physical 
Education from the University of 
Oregon and holds an M.A. degree from 
the same university. Profesor Brown is 
a past president of the B.C. Camping 
Association, Chairman of the Univer¬ 
sity Committee on Camping and Out¬ 
door Education and has had a long 


and varied experience in ail phases of 
camping from counsellor to director to 
committee work. : 

Mrs. May Brown is a graduate ot 
the McGill School of Physical Educa¬ 
tion and holds an M.P.E. degree from 
the University of British Columbia. 
She has professional training in various 
phases of recreation and group work 
with wide experience in camping 
specializing in swimming and water¬ 
front activities. 

Mr. and Mrs. Brown planned and 
taught the Vancouver School Board 
Course in Family Camping for many 
years and currently own and direct 
Camp Deka, located in the beautiful 
and historic Caribou country of British 
Columbia. Camp Deka is a private 
camp for boys situated on Deka Lake 
near Fawn Post Office, Lone Butte, 
B.C, 


CANADIAN CAMPING ASSOCIATION 
NOMINATION PROCEDURE 

The Executive of the Canadian Camping 
Association is elected every two years for a 
two-year term. The present Executive have 
held office for one term of two years. A new 
slate of officers will be elected at the Annual 
Meeting on January 24, 1963, at The 
School of Fine Arts, Banff, Alberta. 

As mentioned by Mr. F." M. Van Wagner, 
Past-President, the Nominating procedure 
outlined in our Constitution has not been 
found practical and, if there is no strong 
opposition, we will continue with the pro¬ 
cedure followed during the last few years. 

Each Provincial Section is urged to survey 
their,.position to determine if they are in a 
position to provide, from their own member¬ 
ship, an Executive to serve the Canadian 
Camping Association for the next two years. 
It would, of course, be necessary to provide 
adequate office accommodation and secre¬ 
tarial services for the office of the Canadian 
Camping Association. 


We urge each Provincial Section that feel 
they can provide an Executive for the Cana¬ 
dian Camping Association to forward to Miss 
Frances Kelly, Executive Secretary, 2233 
Belgrave Avenue, Montreal 28, Quebec, their 
Nominations by Deceniber 15, 1962. They 
should nominate a President, Vice-President, 
Secretary and Treasurer (Provincial Presi¬ 
dents have been namd as the Vice-Presidents 
of the Canadian Camping Association). 

This method has worked very well in the 
past as each local Association, or Branch, 
will know the availability and qualiHcations 
of its members best. 

Although the Alberta Camping Associa¬ 
tion is acting as host for the Canadian 
Camping Association Annual. Meeting, 
Nominations for the Executive of the Cana¬ 
dian Camping Association are open to all 
Provincial Sections, as outlined above, and 
the new Executive will be named at the 
Annual Meeting in January. 

Montreal, Quebec 
September 27, 1962 

KENNETH H. MURRAY 
President

DO YOUR OIL DRUMS LEAK? 

In a conversation with Bill Lecroix 
of Sim Plastics recently, he mentioned 
two novel ideas for adding greater life 
and buoyancy to oil drums used under 
floating docks. 

One method is to fill the drums with 
inexpensive polyurethane foam which 
expands to fill the complete volume of 
the drum. Old age and rust holes in 
the drum will not afTect the buoyancy 
of its contents in the slightest. 


Another idea, even simpler, is to 
carefully insert a large plastic bag 
through the hole in the top of the 
drum. Inflate the plastic bag to fill 
the drum and then tie it off' tightly 
enough to prevent the air from escap¬ 
ing. What you now have is a large 
plastic balloon in.sidc the drum. Once 
again a pin point leak in the drum in 
the future will not affect its buoyancy. 

For further information on the poly¬ 
urethane, contact Bill at SIM PLAS¬ 
TICS. 53 Algie St., Toronto 18.

THE FIVE PENNIES 

By Wendy Phillips 
Counsellor, Camp Oconto 


Everybody has a la\'ouritc song. 
Maybe yours is the camp song, or a 
song you learned when you were little, 
or maybe it’s a beloxed hymn. Mine is 
none of these — it is a song called 
“The Five Pennies.” Rather than sing 
it to you and suddenly find myself 
faced with an^empty chapel, I will tell 
it to you instead. 

This little penny is to wish on, 
d o make your wishes come true. 

This little penny is to dream on, 

'Fo dream of all you can do. 

J'his little penny is a dancing 
penny — 

See how it glitters and it glows! 

As bright as a whistle, sharp as a 
thistle, 

Quick! quick as a wink, up on its 
twinkling toes. 

'This little penny is to laugh on, 

'Vo .see that tears never fall. 

And this little penny is tlie last 
little penny 

And most important of all; 

For this little penny is to love on, 
and where love is, heaven is there. 

So with just five pennies — if 
they’re these five pennies. 

You’ll be a millionaire! 

It’s fun to look at these pennies a 
little more closely to find out what 
they really are saying to us. The first 
little penny is to wish on, to make all 
our wishes come true. I’ll bet that 
down inside we all wish to get some¬ 
thing out of camp. Maybe for you, 
it’s your Red Cross test, or you wish 


you could paddle a canoe or ride a 
horse. Whether we know it or not, 
one thing we all wish for at camp is 
to have a good friend and to be a good 
friend. This little penny hopes that 
some of our wishes come true (for it 
really wouldn’t be right if they all came 
true, would it?) The wishing penny 
hopes that you will get as much out 
of vour few weeks here as you can. 

The second little penny is to dream 
on. Now this doesn't mean that you lie 
on your bed all day dreaming of things 
you’d like to do, but which you say 
you haven’t a ghost of a chance at. 
No, you dream of things you’d like to 
do, then say to yourself that you're 
going to try as hard as you can to 
do them. We should never dream and 
wish about things which are impos¬ 
sible, but we should try really hard to 
fulfil as many of our dreams as we can. 
The next time you think you would 
like to learn the crawl, but you feel 
you could never do it, make a point 
of saying, “I am going to work liard at 
that old crawl,” and soon if you do 
work hard, you’ll find you are making 
your dream come true. 'Fhis is not 
easy to do, but we must never give uj) 
without a good try. 

Next is the dancing penny. Wouldn’t 
it be wonderful if all our faces glowed 
with happiness the way this penny 
glows? It tells us to be as “Bright as a 
whistle.” That means to get as much 
sleep as we need, to trv to stay as 

♦ 


Toronto, Canada, December 1962 


19 


healthy as we can. And “Sharp as a 
thistle” — sharp in making sure we 
don’t hurt other people’s feelings, that 
we help whenever, wherever, whom¬ 
ever we can. “On our twinkling toes” 
we’ll be happy, our minds will be alert, 
and if a gloomy time comes in the day, 
we’ll be able to cheer it up a little. 

The next little penny is to laugh 
on. Counsellors know that campers 
love to laugh — just walk along the 
path after lights out and listen I The 
director knows that the counsellors love 
to laugh by overhearing some of their 
private staff meetings; and everybody 
knows that the director loves to laugh. 
This must be the reason camp is such a 
happy place to be. Smiles are as 
catching as the measles, for when we 
see a person smile, we want to smile 
too. How easy it is to crawl out of bed 
in the morning, grouchy perhaps be¬ 
cause you didn’t have enough sleep; 
but the next time you feel like that, 
tiy humming your favourite song and 
see if the whole section isn’t humming 
— or at least smiling — by breakfast¬ 
time. This penny says, “Laugh and the 
world laughs with you; cry, and you 
ciy alone.” 

The last little penny is most im¬ 
portant of all; it is to love on, and 
where love is heaven is there. Like the 
Bible, this penny is telling us that 
God is love. If we are going to love 
other people, we must treat them the 
way we’d like them to treat us. We 
must respect them for what they are, 
being careful not to hurt their feelings. 
It is so easy to say unkind things to a 
girl or boy whom you don’t like very 
well, but if we all try looking for the 
good things people do, we w'ould for¬ 
get those little bad points which 
everyone has. This last penny wants 
you and me to love each other the way 
God loves us. In doing this, we’ll be 
helping to make the world a happier 
place for everyone. 


Our song ends by saying that if we 
follow the advice of the five pennies 
we shall be a millionaire. This doesn’t 
mean that we’ll have piles and piles of 
money, but that we’ll be rich in the 
things that really count. We’ll be able 
to wish and to dream; we’ll be healthy 
and lively; we’ll laugh and be happy; 
and above all, we will love and be 
loved.

OUR PAL 
JOEY 

A True Story of a Camping Crow 


By Ted Yard 
YMCA Camp Pinecrest 


It’s o\er a year since Joey first ar¬ 
rived at Pine Crest, and started his 
career as pet and entertainer at this 
Y'MCA boy’s summer camp. Since last 
summer however, the great uncertainty 
about his whereabouts and health — if 
indeed he was still alive — had always 
deterred us from telling his story. 

Joey was just a little crow when a 
camper’s parent first brought him to 
us. Unable to fend for himself, he found 
plenty of young friends to pop tasty 
morsels into the gaping beak that 
seemed to hold out a tin cup on many 
a cabin porch rail. Joey thrived on 
attention and good food, and in no 
time flew capably about the Camp on 
his daily “.scrounging mi.ssion.s”, making 
friends wherever he went. 

Among Joey’s friends were two who 
figure largely in the story of his stay 
with us. Sid, the Director of the Junior 
Boys Section Wcis one of these. Joey 
would perch on Sid’s hat or on his 
shoulder and even pick bread out of 
his benefactor’s shirt pocket. Occasion¬ 
ally he’d grab one of the cigars that 
were ever present in this pocket and 
carry it off triumphantly to a secret 
hiding place. Sid was very thoughtful 
of his new-found friend. A dish of 
water on the porch rail, and a genuine 
love for each living creature helped to 
provide the bond between bird and 


man. If they didn’t speak the same 
language they certainly seemed to 
understand one another remarkably 
well! Sitting on Sid’s hat, Joey 
“mugged” his way into a CBC camping 
film shown on the Trans-Canada tele¬ 
vision network — Joey seemed destined 
for fame! 

Soon he found another playmate; 
one whom he could pester and tease; 
one who never tired of chasing after 
him, and one who would never be 
smart enough to catch him! This was 
“Bux/y”, the Camp Director’s dog. 
“Buz/.y” has a somewhat obscure origin, 
but he’s called an “Eskimo hunting 
dog” which .seems to cover most pos¬ 
sibilities! Buzz is as white as Joey is 
black, and early in the season his main 
exercise came from countless futile 
.sorties after scurrying chipmunks and 
squirrels. Then Joey came along! 

Each morning Joe would be waiting 
for Buzz to come out of the cottage. 
With a crackling .squawk he’d flutter to 
the ground dragging a suppo.sedly 
broken wing, and when the pup bound¬ 
ed after him, Joe would take off, flying 
low over Buzzy’s head and laughing 
his most taunting laugh! Buzz would 
take up the chase, usually oblivious to 
where Joe was leading him, and on 
more than one occasion the wiley low- 


Toronto, Canada, December 1962 


21 


flying joker took him right oil the 
dock into the lakel Several times Joe 
tried to lead his playmate over a high 
rock ledge, but always the pup sensed 
the danger just in time. 

All-in-all the crow had a hilarious 
time! On the football field he would 
strut around pecking at the soccer hall 
and acting like an international centre 
forward — until Buzz arrived to send 
him “to the showers”. 

When Camp closed last year the 
crow missed the children’s attention 
and decided to concentrate on torment¬ 
ing Buzzy. One evening, just before 
Labour Day, he’d been u|3 to his old 
tricks. Swooping low through a stand 
of liemlocks he laughed hilariously at 
the pup whom he had again so easily 
outwitted. But his laugh trailed ofi' into 
a wild cackle as he banged scpiarely 
into one of the trees and fell to the 
ground! Buzzy ran right over him 
and was several yards past before he 
could pull up to a stop. By this time 
joey had struggled uj) and lumbered 
over to a bridge rail where he sulkily 
surveyed the site of his near demise. 
'Fhat dejected picture was our last 
glimpse of him. Was he hurt badly? 
Did a hawk get him? Did he go .south? 
We often wondered. 


I'his .sea.son many caiuj^ers have 
asked about Joey. While we had little 
hope, we really didn’t know what had 
happened to him, so we always said, 
“probably some day he will be back 
again.” 

At noon on August 16, Sid came into 
the dining hall looking something like 
a bishop who had just won a raffle. A 
rumor rumbled around the tables light¬ 
ing u|) the faces of all who heard it. 
riien a black shadow swooped by the 
front of the building. There on his old 
ledge was our pal Joey! 


During the winter he had acquired 
a new cry strangely like that of a child 
calling “mama”, and now he picked 
up right where he had left off with the 
campers and with the pup. 

To-night as 1 write this, Joey is 
crestfallen! Three wing feathers on the 
ground bear mute evidence to his latest 
brash escapade. During the supper hour 
he had perched in a tree by the dining 
hall apparently enjoying one of our 
ten-minute Muskoka showers. Then, 
forgetting that his wings were wet, he 
dropped down to tease the pup again. 
Buzzy caught his tormentor and 
gathered in three black chevrons. Joey, 
his pride sorely wounded, fled to a 
nearby tree scolding profanely. This is 
a little reminiscent of last season’s end. 
But we hope, somehow, that this season 
the trickster will be a better sport, 
swallow his jDridc, and stay around 
camp, oh — quite a bit longer!

Revel in a life of sin 
Caring little for the sorrow

Brothers to the brutish swine. 

Wives there be who kill their husbands, 
Putting poison in their tea; 

Men there be who slay their women— 
Push them overboard at .sea! 

But the meanest of these vermin. 
Though through all the world you 
search

2. I suggest to you that the equip¬ 
ment, maintenance and instruction 
necessary for compressed air diving 
may be too complicated for most 
directors. The refilling of tanks may be 
quite a problem in the camp areas, 
and the necessity of regular inspection 
on this equipment is very' important, 
considering the number of different 
users that may be involved. 

3. Under d i v i n g club circum¬ 
stances, vve have no liesitation in re¬ 
commending instruction for air equip¬ 
ment to younger people (say 12 to 16 
years) who are satisfactoiy insofar as 
their fitness, swimming ability and 
medical certificate are concerned. The 
obtaining of qualified instructors to 
teach on diving with air at camps may 
be difficult, and this fact plus the 
question of equipment might deter 
most directors. If qualified instructors 
are available, and the equipment and 
airfill situation is not a problem, then 
by all means make use of the new 
s|)ort as an activity. It is truly a 
fasci nating experience. 

4. The teaching of basic equip¬ 
ment, i.e. fins, mask and snorkel, can 
be carried on with much less effort on 
the part of the camp and can provide 
a really exciting activity. 

In short, there is really^ no reason 
why the use of compressed air for 
diving cannot be taught as an activity 
to older boys—and I would say' 14 to 16 
years as some physics is involved and 
the really’ y'oung ones do not compre¬ 
hend — provided proper equipment 
and instructors are available. 

Basic equipment diving might be 
more attractive to most camp people 
but the quality of instruction must not 
be less than that required for air 
diving.”

up your skill and zeal with some read¬ 
ing in the winter months? Or are you 
fairly new to the job of directing a 
camp? We have for you here a list of 
books recommended by a group of 
experienced camp directors. They re¬

bership to whom we wrote, asking each 
of them to choose twelve books they 
would consider essential to a - camp 
director’s bookshelf. Our thank you to 
those who have responded. This list 
is confined to the titles they contri¬ 
buted. Some titles appeared on only 
one director’s selection.

place across the width of the excava¬ 
tion, allowing the ends to project up 
and over the rim of the excavation. 
The edges of each succeeding strip 
were oxerlapped four inches, and 
cemented with a cold tar cement 
purcha.sed from the manufacturer of 
the liner material. Long-handled 
brushes facilitated this operation and 
a warm day — although harder on the 
workers — made handling the liner 
easier. Any unevenness, fullne.ss. 
wrinkles or bulges are easily removed 
by slitting the liner with a knife or 
shears and patching with a piece oi 
liner and cement. Fitting around the 
corners was accomplished by the same 
method of slitting and overlapping the 
cut (*dges of the liner. 

Having completed the first layer of 
liner over the entire pool surface and 
cemented it to the drain outlet in the 
bottom, we placed a row of 10” cement 
blocks around the perimeter of the 
rim of the excavation about 8 indies 
below the level of the top ol the pool 
wall. This row of blocks serves to hold 
the first layer of liner in place. 

The .second layer of liner is placed at 
a 45 degree angle to the first, each 
strip is overlapped four inches and 
cemented to the preceding layer. The 
ends of each stri|) are brought up and 
over the row of cement blocks and 
cemented to them. At this point a 
second row of 8 inch concrete blocks 
is placed on top of the first row. Our 
engineer, Mr. Doug. E. Smith, recom¬ 
mended that at intervals pre-cast 8 
inch scum gutters — whicli we cast 
on the job — form part of this layer 
of blocks. These scum gutters are con¬ 
nected to the pumping .system and help 
take ofl' surface contamination. 

I'he third and final layer of liner 
was then applied at a 45 degree angle 
to the precei'ding layer. 4'he ends were 


26 


Canadian Campino 




brought well up and over the blocks at 
the rim of the pool. A sectional cement 
slab walk three feet wide was cast on 
the job and placed to hold the project¬ 
ing ends of the liner in place. This 
gives a finished effect to the pool and 
provides a cement walk around the 
perimeter. 

The entire liner was painted with 
two coats of light blue latex paint, and 
the pool had the appearance and. 
utility of a concrete pool. A standard 
circulating swimming pool pump was 
obtained and installed with the neces¬ 
sary valves, piping, chlorinator, and a 
sand and gravel filter unit. 

The pool was built during the 
summer of 1961. Water was left in it 
during the winter without damage. 
Ladders for entry and exit were added 
in 1962 and a protective fence was 
built around the pool. During the 1962 
season the pool was used successfully 
and it gives every indication of a 
useful life equal to the more expensive 
concrete pools. It is very like a concrete 
pool in appearance, is certainly less 
expensive, it can be built on a do it 
yourself basis, and we believe will re¬ 
quire less upkeep over the years to 
come. 


The Camper and the Birthday Suit 
by MARY EDGAR 

Once there was a camper 
Whose first letter to her home 
Amazed her doting parents 
And inspired this little “pome**. 

(She wrote): 

Dear Mum and Dad: Got here O.K., 
Please send a box of food. 

My cabin mates inform me 
There is swimming “a la nude”. 
They say my bathing suit won’t do, 
It’s not the kind they wear; 

Please buy for me a Birthday Suit, 
And Rush it here by air. 


WMesaie

Toronto, Canada, December 1962 


27 



CAMP 

CAP3RS 


Traditionally, the time for camp 
capers is the last morning of camp^ 
Long before rising bell (like about 15 
minutes) the camp resounds to the 
merry laughter of the young, and the 
low-pitched moans of the not-so-young 
who have just looked at their watches. 

But this year, all was deathly still. 
No sound of jollity, gaiety or song 
and dance. Too soon I congratulated 
myself that the tradition had been for¬ 
gotten or replaced by a more adult one 
(like sleeping in). 

As I rounded the corner of the 
Lodge, there, ranged about the flag¬ 
pole in a perfect hollow square was the 
footgear of evei^^ camper in camp. 
Drawn up in perfectly straight lines 
were junior rubber boots, senior thongs, 
intermediate penny loafers or desert 
boots. Many unwary counsellors were 
represented too — some of them, I 
was amused to note —r.with two left 
feet (a thing I often had suspected). 

When the bell went for flag-raising, 
no campers turned up. The counsellors 
solemnly raised the flag and went in 
to breakfast, and following them was 
a laughing gang of children who 
seemed to come out of the woodwork. 

Joyce Bertram, Camp Ouareau. 


What were so7ne of the ^amp capers 
that happened at your camp over the years? 
The editorial committee would welcome 
contributions to this new series. 


As long as we continue to hire lively 
imaginative young people as counsel¬ 
lors, we will always have “high jinks’* 
at camp. As long as these capers are 
not malicious, vandaloiis or inconsider¬ 
ate, they can add zest to camp life. 

While visiting an Ontario camp this 
summer, an incomparably beautiful 
site with numerous bays and islands, 
I was taken on a tour of the lake by 
boat. Suddenly rounding a point, we 
came upon a tiny island, a rather 
ordinary rocky island about 10 feet 
square but also quite unique, for 
parked on it was a car that covered 
most of the island. Nothing could have 
looked more incongruous. 

“How did a car get out into the 
middle of the lake onto this tiny 
island?” I asked my guide. He just 
shrugged his shoulders and gave me a 
faint grin. 

Everyone I asked during my visit 
just shrugged their shoulders which 
only heightened my curiosity, for how 
was a full sized automobile moved 
across a mile of water without anyone 
being aware of it. 

Finally, as I was leaving I asked once 
more and the young man answered, 
“This is called a lesson in humility, 
just to make the director aware of the 
fact that he doesn’t really know 
EVERYTHING that happens at 
camp.” 

Barry Lowes, Camp Timberlane 



28 


Canadian Campino 



from page 10 


sound, can find opportunity daily to 
render those services to one’s fellow 
man (c.g. Kindness, consideration etc.) 
which our Judaeo-Christian tradition 
dictates as obligations. In short, he is a 
person at camp who must be concerned 
about his relationship with his fellow 
persons. In this way he too finds a 
means of strengthening his relationship 
with his Creator. Directing a camp 
provides ample opportunity for one to 
grow in this aspect. 

To the author, as well, directing a 
camp offers scope for one’s creative 
ability. Season by season, because of 
the nature of our camping structure, it 
is necessaiy to develop and build a 
team of personnel who will comprise 
the camp community. The task of 
structuring cabin groups; of developing 
a staff and camper network of com¬ 
munications; of providing opportunity 
lor individual and group skills and 
abilities to be used in the camp activ¬ 
ities; offers scope to an individual as he 
watclies h i s community-in-miniature 
grow. Surely no time and no oppor¬ 
tunity such as that afl'orded by a camp 
can offer so much room for creative 
effort on the part of the director who.se 
j)rime responsibility is that of organiz¬ 
ing the total camp scene. 

We began by saying there is a magic 
in camping—the magic of pine trees 
silhouetted against a glowing sunset — 
a magic in the warm excitement of 
accomplishing things together; magic 
kindled by an expression of gratitude 
and affection in the eyes of a camper; 
and the wizardry in the unfolding of a 
sea.son’s preparations and planning. 

A magic which year upon year trans¬ 
forms a winter’s pen into a paddle and 
this “desk-jockey” into a Camp 
Director!
